newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bank of Baroda sees 97/98 net up 40 pct.
newsitem.headline: India's Bank of Baroda sees 97/98 net up 40 pct.

text.p: India's state-run Bank of Baroda expects to post a 40 percent rise in net profit in 1997/98 (April-March), its chairman said on Tuesday.
The bank posted a 33 percent rise in net profit at 2.76 billion rupees for the year ended March 31, 1997, chairman K. Kannan told a news conference.

Bank officials said its operations this year will show the favourable impact of a reduction in deposit rates. It will also have the advantage of funds raised from a public issue of shares late last year, they said.
The bank is targeting a 50 billion-rupee rise in deposits and a 35 billion increase in advances this year, officials said.

"We are gearing up to meet full convertibility," an official said, referring to the recent publication of a report commissioned by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on making the rupee fully convertible on the capital account by 2000.
The bank, which has branches in several countries, has 27.0 billion rupees in foreign currency deposits.
During 1996/97, the bank raised the capital adequacy ratio to 11.8 percent from 11.2 percent a year ago.
Return on assets improved to 0.78 percent from 0.65 percent, return on net worth to 16.68 percent from 11.80 percent and earnings per share to 10.87 rupees from 3.61 rupees.
The bank's global deposits reached 321.57 billion rupees against 283.7 billion rupees a year ago. Advances in 1996/97 rose to 165.32 billion rupees from 160.13 billion.
Investments this year amounted to 109.27 billion rupees compared to 96.21 billion a year ago, a bank statement said.
Kannan said the bank's interest spread came under pressure in the falling interest rate scenario. The spread fell to 3.9 percent against 3.84 percent in the previous year.
The bank said it is making efforts to make good the loss by improving the non-interest income though not much success could be achieved last year due to an adverse environment.

It said the bank's performance was up despite a subdued growth in non-fund business because of low export-import growth and a marginal rise in non-performing assets caused by an industrial slowdown and various court orders affecting several industries.
The bank returned 3.81 billion rupees of recapitalisation bonds to the government with interest, Kannan said.
